opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. One distinction I keep returning to is between AI that can do a *task* and AI that can do a whole *job*. In our surveys of AI researchers we asked about both. One question was when machines could accomplish every task better and more cheaply than human workers. A separate question was when all occupations would be fully automatable. In principle those should land in roughly the same place, because a job is just a bundle of tasks. In practice researchers gave much later dates for full automation of occupations, sometimes by many decades. That gap tells you something, even if it's partly a framing effect.

I think the gap reflects how much of the work in a job isn't captured in a list of discrete tasks. There's the stitching together, knowing which task matters right now, and handling the weird exception. There's being accountable when something goes wrong, and holding context across months. So an AI can be superhuman at many of the pieces of a job while the job itself still has a person in it, at least for a while.

That connects to a second distinction: assisting versus replacing. When AI assists, the human is still the one deciding what's worth doing, and the AI makes them faster or better. When it automates, the human is out of the loop. The economic and social effects differ a lot depending on which one you're in. Assistance can make workers more valuable. Automation can make them unnecessary for that function.

The part I find most important, and a bit neglected, is that the line between the two can move quickly and quietly. You start with a tool that drafts and a person who checks. Over time, people check less carefully because the tool is usually right. Eventually nobody really checks, and you've drifted into automation without ever deciding to. So I'd want people to notice where on that spectrum they actually are, rather than where they think they are, especially for decisions that matter.

r001.rationale: The response says that as the tool is usually right, people check less, until nobody really checks. This clearly conveys the practical threshold where reliability leads to no longer reviewing each execution.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the distinction I keep coming back to is between AI that helps you do something and AI that does the thing instead of you, and which one you end up with isn't really a technical fact about the system, it's about where the human sits in the loop and what they're still required to understand.

So, for instance, if I'm writing something and I use a model to tighten a paragraph, I'm still the one who knows what I'm trying to say, and I can tell whether the output is right. That's assistance. The understanding stays with me. But if I ask it to write the whole piece and I just skim it and send it, then functionally the task has been automated, even though I'm nominally still "using a tool." And I think people often don't notice when they've crossed that line, because the interface looks the same in both cases.

Why does it matter practically? A few reasons. One is that in the assistance case, errors tend to get caught, because there's a person who actually knows the domain checking the work. In the automation case, you've quietly removed that check, and you often don't find out until something goes wrong. Another is about what happens to skills over time. If you're using AI to do the parts you already understand, you stay competent. If you're using it to skip the parts you never learned, you end up in a position where you can't evaluate what it's giving you, and you can't take the task back if the system stops being available or starts being wrong.

And I think there's a bigger version of this that matters for how AI goes in general. A lot of the arguments for why things will be fine assume humans remain meaningfully in control, that we're being assisted rather than replaced in the relevant decisions. But if the default behavior of individuals and organizations is to drift toward automation whenever it's cheaper and locally fine, then that assumption erodes one small choice at a time, without anyone deciding it. So I'd want people to actually ask, for a given task: do I still know what's happening here, and could I notice if it were wrong? If the answer is no, you've automated it, and you should at least be doing that on purpose.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes assistance from automation by whether the person understands and can evaluate the work, and says automation removes the human check. It does not identify reliability sufficient to stop reviewing each execution as the threshold.

astra-6.text:
I think a useful distinction is between AI that helps you do a task and AI that can take responsibility for the whole task. If it produces something that you then have to check carefully, you’re still quite involved. And how useful that is depends a lot on how easy it is to check the result relative to doing the task yourself.

If you can hand something off and trust that it will get done, that’s a different situation. So I’m interested in how much human attention is still required, rather than just whether the AI can produce an impressive answer.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts outputs that require careful checking with tasks that can be handed off and trusted, identifying reduced need for human review as the practical threshold.

sol-6.1.text: I think an important distinction is between helping you do a task and being able to take responsibility for the whole task. An AI might make individual steps much faster, but if you still have to decide what to ask it, check everything, and fix the mistakes, then you’re still quite involved. If you can hand it a task and reliably get back a finished result, that changes how much human labor is needed. So I’d look at how much supervision remains, rather than just whether the AI can do the impressive-looking parts.

r001.rationale: The response describes handing off a task and reliably receiving a finished result, with little or no remaining supervision, rather than checking every step.
